sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: Answer in one word: (I) What is the method of voting used in the election of the President of India? (II) For how long can the Vice-President act as President in the absence of a sitting President?
questions.answer: (I) Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (secret ballot) (II) Six months

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain the number of judges, including the Chief Justice, in the Supreme Court of India.
questions.answer: The Constitution provides a Chief Justice and other judges whose number is fixed by Parliament by law. In 1950 there was a Chief Justice and 7 judges; the number has been increased with need — the textbook gives a Chief Justice and 30 judges.

questions.q: Explain the importance of a no-confidence motion in the Indian Parliament in two points.
questions.answer: (1) It is the strongest way the Lok Sabha controls the executive: if passed, the Prime Minister and the entire Council of Ministers must resign, because they are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. (2) It keeps the government accountable and alert, since it must keep majority support (e.g. Vajpayee's government fell in 1999).

questions.q: Mention any two qualifications required to be elected as President of India.
questions.answer: (1) Must be a citizen of India who has completed 35 years of age. (2) Must be qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha and must not hold any office of profit under the Union, a State or a local authority.

questions.q: Describe any two powers of the Prime Minister related to the Council of Ministers.
questions.answer: (1) The President appoints ministers and allocates portfolios on the PM's recommendation, so the PM makes and unmakes the Council. (2) The PM presides over Cabinet meetings and coordinates ministers; if the PM resigns the whole Council stands dissolved.

questions.q: How do both Houses of Parliament maintain control over the Council of Ministers? Highlight two ways.
questions.answer: (1) Members ask questions and supplementary questions in Question Hour, which ministers must answer. (2) They move calling-attention, adjournment and censure motions to debate and criticise policies; the Lok Sabha can also reject the budget or pass a no-confidence motion.

questions.q: Differentiate between direct and indirect elections in India with examples.
questions.answer: In a direct election the people themselves vote for representatives — e.g. members of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. In an indirect election elected representatives choose the person — e.g. the President (by an Electoral College) and Rajya Sabha members (by MLAs).

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain any three executive powers of the President of India.
questions.answer: (1) Appoints the Prime Minister and, on the PM's advice, other ministers; all executive action is in his/her name. (2) Appoints Governors, the Attorney General, the CAG, ambassadors, the UPSC, the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts and Election Commissioners, and can remove many of them as provided. (3) Is Supreme Commander of the armed forces and appoints the three service chiefs; treaties are concluded in his/her name.

questions.q: Explain the functions of the Prime Minister.
questions.answer: (1) Forms the Council of Ministers and allocates portfolios; presides over the Cabinet and coordinates ministers. (2) Is the link between the President and the Council of Ministers, communicating all decisions, and may advise dissolution of the Lok Sabha. (3) Leads Parliament and the nation, defends government policy, chairs the Planning Commission/NITI Aayog and NDC, and represents India abroad.

questions.q: Explain the emergency powers of the President of India.
questions.answer: (1) National emergency for war, external aggression or armed rebellion — only on the Cabinet's written decision; approved by Parliament within a month; the Centre can direct States and Fundamental Rights may be suspended. (2) President's Rule (Art. 356) when a State's constitutional machinery fails — the Governor rules on the President's behalf and Parliament legislates for the State; maximum three years. (3) Financial emergency when India's financial stability is threatened — salaries, even of judges, can be cut; never declared so far.

questions.q: Explain the financial powers of the President of India.
questions.answer: (1) No money bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha without the President's recommendation. (2) The annual budget (Annual Financial Statement) is laid before Parliament with his/her consent before each financial year. (3) In a financial emergency he/she can reduce the salaries of government servants, including Supreme Court and High Court judges.

questions.q: Describe the close relationship between the legislature and the executive in India.
questions.answer: (1) The executive (PM and ministers) are members of Parliament and must become MPs within six months. (2) The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and stays only while it has majority support — a no-confidence motion removes it. (3) Parliament controls the executive through Question Hour, motions and approval of the budget, while the PM can advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Explain the functions (jurisdiction) of the Supreme Court of India.
questions.answer: (1) Original jurisdiction — disputes between the Union and States or between States. (2) Appellate jurisdiction — appeals in constitutional, civil and criminal cases from High Courts; special leave to appeal. (3) Advisory jurisdiction — opinion on matters referred by the President. It is also a court of record, the guardian of the Constitution and Fundamental Rights, and exercises judicial review.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain any six legislative powers of the President.
questions.answer: (1) The President is an integral part of Parliament. (2) Summons and prorogues the sessions of both Houses. (3) Dissolves the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Council of Ministers. (4) Addresses Parliament at the first session each year and after each general election. (5) No bill becomes law without his/her assent; he/she may return a bill for reconsideration. (6) Calls a joint sitting to resolve deadlocks, issues ordinances when Parliament is not in session, and nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.

or.q: Explain the meaning of the Electoral College in the Indian Presidential election. What qualifications are required for a person to be elected President of India?
or.answer: Electoral College: the body that elects the President indirectly — the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry). Voting is by secret ballot using proportional representation by single transferable vote. Qualifications: (1) citizen of India; (2) at least 35 years old; (3) qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha; (4) not holding any office of profit under the Union, a State or local authority. The term is five years, with re-election allowed.

questions.q: Explain the powers of the Supreme Court of India.
questions.answer: (1) Original jurisdiction over disputes between the Union and States or among States. (2) Appellate jurisdiction — the highest court of appeal in constitutional, civil and criminal cases; special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal; can review its own judgments. (3) Advisory jurisdiction on matters referred by the President. (4) Court of record — its judgments bind all lower courts. (5) Guardian of the Constitution and protector of Fundamental Rights through writs (Article 32). (6) Judicial review — declares laws and orders that violate the Constitution null and void; judicial activism through PIL gives the poor access to justice.

or.q: Explain the powers of the Prime Minister of India.
or.answer: (1) Real head of the Union executive; the President acts on the binding advice of the Council headed by the PM. (2) Recommends appointment of ministers, allocates and reshuffles portfolios, and can ask ministers to resign. (3) Presides over the Cabinet and coordinates all ministries. (4) Link between the President and the Council of Ministers; advises dissolution of the Lok Sabha. (5) Leader of the majority, of Parliament and of the nation; chief spokesperson of government policy. (6) Chairs the Planning Commission/NITI Aayog and NDC, takes decisions on defence and foreign policy and represents India abroad — the 'keystone of the cabinet arch'.

questions.q: Describe the functions of the Indian Parliament.
questions.answer: (1) Legislative: makes laws on the Union and Concurrent Lists and residuary subjects; joint sitting for deadlocks. (2) Control over the executive: Question Hour, motions and the no-confidence motion. (3) Financial: passes the budget; no tax or expenditure without its approval; money bills start in the Lok Sabha. (4) Judicial: fixes the number of Supreme Court judges and removes judges by impeachment. (5) Electoral: takes part in electing the President and elects the Vice-President. (6) Constituent: amends the Constitution and impeaches the President.
